claim: Practitioner exit bands: dropshipping stores sell for about 1 to 2x EBITDA, ordinary ecom brands about 3 to 6x, and rare brands with retail and a product flywheel far more.
body: The founder gives rough exit multiples, explaining that ecom valuations fell after many listed ecom brands dropped, because low barriers to entry make the model easy to disrupt. His bands: a dropshipping store about 1 to 2 times EBITDA; a branded ecom business about 3 to 6 times EBITDA, with category type (he names beauty and supplements, linked to replenishment) affecting where it lands; outliers with retail distribution, a clear product flywheel and a strong following can reach about 3 to 5 times revenue or 30 times EBITDA. He warns owners not to assume they are the outlier. The host adds that market timing moves multiples a lot, citing an agency sold in 2021 at 11 times profit against a more usual six or so. How to use it: value on EBITDA by default, and treat a revenue multiple as earned only by distribution, repeat purchase and brand pull. He also mentions a $130M offer for Oodie that collapsed. These are spoken ranges, not a transaction dataset, and the category condition is loosely worded in the transcript.
conditions: Private sale of an ecom brand; multiples quoted around 2025 in an Australian and UK context; EBITDA-based valuation.
fails_when: Buyer market is hot (multiples rise sharply, as in 2021) or frozen; the business has unusual recurring revenue or strategic value to a specific acquirer; a revenue-based deal for a high-growth brand.

branded ecom about 3 to 6x EBITDA
outliers about 3 to 5x revenue or about 30x EBITDA
agency sold in 2021 at 11x profit versus about 6x usual

topics: chart of accounts and P&L structure
claim: In US grocery retail, retailers take 45 to 50% of shelf price, distributors 15 to 25%, trade spend 20 to 30%, so build on 50%+ gross margin.
body: Ross McKay, founder of electrolyte drink brand Cadence (about $10M revenue in roughly 600 days, entering Target and Walmart), lays out the waterfall a DTC founder rarely sees until the first retail meeting. Start from the recommended shelf price (his can is $2.79 at Target; Walmart usually lowest). Retailers generally want 45 to 50% margin, so your sell-in price is roughly shelf price minus 50%. From that you subtract distribution and freight. If you use a distributor, their margin runs 15 to 25%. Then the line he says nobody talks about: trade spend, typically 20 to 30% of revenue, covering promotions, end caps, demos and price cuts. On a two-for-$4 promotion against a $2.50 everyday price, the brand usually funds 50 to 100% of the dollar off, often for 60 to 120 days, or around 12 weeks, a year. His rule: in CPG you want to be building from a 50%+ gross margin at sell-in price before trade spend, or retail will eat you. How to apply: before pitching a retailer, build the full waterfall per unit (shelf price, retailer cut, distributor cut, freight, trade spend at 25%) and check contribution margin is still positive at your current COGS.
conditions: US mass and grocery retail (Target, Walmart, grocery, specialty like GNC), consumable CPG with a low shelf price; figures as stated by one founder in beverage.
fails_when: Direct-to-store distribution without a distributor (removes the 15 to 25% layer); specialty or boutique retail with different margin norms; categories where retailers buy on consignment or marketplace terms; non-US markets.

topics: funding options and cost of capital
claim: A dividend recap needs roughly $2M+ EBITDA for three years with the last audited; lenders lend about 3x EBITDA at 12 to 14% effective, with interest cover of 2x.
body: Khan describes the dividend recapitalisation private equity uses, applied to a profitable DTC brand. The company (not the founder) borrows against its earnings and pays the cash out to owners. Thresholds he gives for today's market: at least about $2M EBITDA, sustained for three years, with the most recent year audited. Typical size is about 3x EBITDA (so $6M on $2M). Cost: a term sheet might say 10%, but break fees, admin costs, a quality-of-earnings review and maintenance push the effective rate to 12 to 14%; at about $10M EBITDA it can fall to 9 to 11%, without warrants or equity. Interest is deductible, so the after-tax cost is lower (he estimates 6 to 8% at roughly 30% tax). The main covenant is interest cover: lenders want earnings of about twice the annual interest; for a $10M loan at 10% ($1M interest), profits must stay above about $2M or the loan is in breach and the lender can take control. Large borrowers get down to 1.5x. Lenders often prefer a recap alongside new equity, and some may require partial recourse or personal guarantees. A brand bought with no debt can be recapped immediately.
conditions: Profitable DTC companies with $2M+ EBITDA and audited accounts; US-style corporate lending market (he references a C corp); stable or growing earnings.
fails_when: Volatile earnings that can breach interest-cover covenants (ad cost spikes, tariff shocks); brands needing the cash for growth; founders without audited history; lenders demanding personal guarantees; confirm structure and tax with an accountant.
numbers: Minimum ~$2M EBITDA for 3 years, last year audited
Borrow ~3x EBITDA
Effective cost 12 to 14% (10% headline); 9 to 11% at ~$10M EBITDA
After-tax cost ~6 to 8% at ~30% tax
Interest cover covenant ~2x (as low as 1.5x for very large borrowers)

topics: funding options and cost of capital
claim: Chinese factories can fund net 90+ terms by factoring your invoices under export credit insurance at about 6% APR; offer to share that cost on the BOM.
body: Mechanism as Khan describes it for a large Chinese jewellery factory (about $300M a year across 100+ brands): the factory pays a credit insurer (he names Sinosure and Allianz) an annual premium; the insurer sends each buyer a light audit request (management accounts, P&L, past payment disputes or bankruptcies) and grades the buyer A, B or C. The factory then sells your invoice to a bank (Bank of China, HSBC and others) at about 99 cents on the dollar for 90 to 180 days, which he puts at roughly 6% a year in China (higher in Thailand, where he later moved production because of tariffs). Put that financing cost on the BOM as its own line: on $12M of purchases that was about $600k, roughly $6 a unit on 100,000 units, falling as volume rises. Then negotiate the split: he paid 80% and the factory 20% while the brand was cash-constrained, and the relationship later moved to consignment. A poor grade blocks this: his brand was rated C over a supplier dispute about eight years earlier and had to clean up its books first. His comparison: revenue-based financing quoted around 10% can become 30 to 40% effective when you grow fast, so supplier finance is cheap at low single digits of revenue.
conditions: Brands buying meaningful volume ($ millions a year) from Chinese or Southeast Asian exporters; clean payment history; open-book BOM relationship.
fails_when: Small buyers below insurers' and banks' thresholds; buyers with disputes or late payments on record (C grade); factories outside export-credit schemes; rates differ by country and change with interest rates.
numbers: Invoice factoring ~1% per 90 days, ~6% APR in China
$12M purchases -> ~$600k financing cost (~$6/unit on 100k units)
Financing cost split 80/20 brand/factory in his case
Revenue-based loans: ~10% nominal can reach 30 to 40% effective with fast growth

claim: Supplier float equals payment terms minus production-to-warehouse lead time; net 90 with a 30-day lead time gives 60 days, and consignment, paying only when units sell, is the ideal.
body: Khan's framing: overhead is predictable and marketing can be switched off with a click, but a purchase order cannot be cancelled, so COGS timing is the main free-cash-flow risk. Float is payment terms minus the time to make the goods and get them into your warehouse. Net 90 with 30 days to warehouse gives 60 days of float; many brands sit at net 30 to 45 with 45 to 90 days to land stock, which is negative float. Real float is lower still because buying mistakes (too many size 7 rings, not enough 9s) leave stock on the balance sheet. Two ways to buy: outright, where you own inventory once the PO is invoiced, and consignment, where the factory places goods in your warehouse and you pay only as they sell, giving the cash profile of drop shipping on a custom product. He has true consignment for jewellery (gold has high remelt value and inventory sits in Hong Kong where recourse is easy). At Raycon the invoice says net 90 for the factory's financing, but in practice the brand pays weekly every Friday against sell-through, so excess inventory is never fully on the brand. With wide float he says a business growing 80% needs close to zero extra working capital, and he distributes 65 to 75% of monthly free cash flow after closing management accounts by the 15th of each month.
conditions: DTC brands buying manufactured inventory from overseas factories; brands with enough volume and clean payment history to negotiate terms; global mechanics, but tax and legal set-up varies.
fails_when: New or small brands without credit history (factories ask for deposits up front); products with low resale or recourse value, making consignment unacceptable to the supplier; long-tail SKU complexity that eats the float through overstock.
numbers: Float = payment terms - lead time to warehouse (net 90 - 30 days = 60 days)
Typical brand: net 30 to 45 terms vs 45 to 90 day lead times
Raycon: weekly Friday payments against a net 90 invoice
Distributes 65 to 75% of monthly free cash flow; books closed by the 15th

claim: A sourcing agent can fund a year's supply at volume pricing on top of your usual order, then sell it to you as used, removing lead time and MOQ.
body: A US sourcing agent and contract manufacturer describes a structure for brands that cannot afford volume discounts. Baseline terms: the brand pays 30% deposit to start production and 70% before shipment, reordering several times a year at a landed cost of, say, 10.00 per unit. When the next order is due, the agent adds his own money to lift the order to a full year's supply. The brand's units still cost 10.00; the agent's extra units cost him less because the larger order unlocked a volume price (and often cheaper consolidated freight). The whole year's supply ships to the brand's warehouse. Once the brand sells through the units it paid for, it buys from the agent's stock already on site at the same 10.00, paying only as it uses inventory, with no lead time and no MOQ. The agent's margin is the volume discount. How to apply: 1) List discounts you leave unused because of cash flow (volume tiers, consolidated freight). 2) Approach your agent, a distributor or an inventory investor with this split. 3) Agree storage, insurance, ownership of goods in your warehouse and what happens to unsold stock. The commenter says the cash-flow benefit can be worth more than the discount itself.
conditions: Brands reordering a stable SKU several times a year with predictable demand and warehouse space; agents or investors willing to hold stock.
fails_when: Demand is uncertain or the product may change, leaving a year of stock unsold and the agreement in dispute; unclear title to goods in your warehouse creates legal and accounting risk (confirm with an accountant); jurisdiction-specific rules on consignment stock apply.
numbers: typical terms 30% deposit, 70% before shipment
example landed cost 10.00 per unit
agent tops order up to a 1-year supply

claim: COGS is 'all in until it's in': purchase price, inbound freight, container and import duty allocated per unit; outbound shipping, platform fees, ads and 3PL storage sit below gross profit.
body: Phil Oakley of Outserve, an accounting integrator for Amazon and Shopify brands, gives the working rule: every cost to get the product from the supplier's door onto your shelf ready to sell is cost of goods sold; every cost after that point is an operating expense. A second test: would you have incurred this cost if you had not bought this shipment? Container freight and import duty, no, so COGS; warehouse rent, yes, so overhead. In COGS: purchase price (net of supplier discounts), inbound freight, container cost, import duties and tariffs. Not in COGS: outbound shipping to customers, Amazon and Shopify fees, PPC and other advertising, 3PL storage and pick-pack. Two exceptions he names: drop-ship suppliers who bill a bundled outbound freight charge, and products sold with free shipping built into the price, where outbound shipping can be treated as COGS. The most common failure he sees is lump-sum freight and duty invoices never allocated to the products they belonged to. Best practice: capture freight and duty against the purchase order when it is raised and weight it across the lines (by value, weight or volume) to get a landed cost per unit; spreadsheets work early, inventory software as you scale.
conditions: Brands that buy finished goods in (not manufacturers, which add a further cost layer); statutory accounts; confirm treatment with your accountant.

topics: chart of accounts and P&L structure
claim: Packaging splits two ways: the branded retail box is COGS, the plain shipping carton it travels in is a shipping expense, even when both appear on one supplier invoice.
body: Oakley's packaging test: is it part of the product as it would sit on a retail shelf, or is it there to ship it? The product box with the picture on it, inner packaging and inserts that form the product people buy are part of cost of goods sold, like the white box an iPhone comes in. The brown carton, mailer, void fill and tape it goes into when it leaves the warehouse are costs incurred after the sale and belong in shipping or fulfilment expense, below gross profit. In practice a packaging supplier often bills both on the same invoice, so the bookkeeper has to split the lines rather than post the whole invoice to one account. Why it matters: posting mailers to COGS depresses gross margin and makes products look less profitable than they are, while posting retail boxes to shipping inflates gross margin and understates landed unit cost, which then feeds wrong break-even ROAS and pricing. How to apply: set up separate accounts or SKUs for product packaging and shipping packaging, map each packaging line on supplier invoices, and include product packaging in the landed cost per unit.
conditions: Ecommerce brands with branded product packaging plus separate shipping materials; confirm with your accountant.

claim: Return shipping is an overhead, but labour and materials to repackage or refurbish a returned item for resale go into COGS; coupons reduce revenue, not COGS.
body: Oakley separates the two halves of a return. Bringing the item back, the return label and carrier cost, is an expense after the sale and sits in overheads. Making the item sellable again (new product box, repackaging, refurbishing) is a cost of getting stock back onto the shelf and can be classified as cost of goods sold. Related lines: a supplier discount on purchased goods reduces COGS; a supplier credit for returned stock moves with the stock; a customer coupon reduces the sale price and therefore revenue, not COGS, while advertising and Amazon PPC are operating expenses. He notes that for management reporting, apparel brands with heavy returns often track additional margin views (contribution margin after returns, cost of returns per order) alongside statutory gross margin, and that return-to-exchange offers (vouchers, trade-ups, prepaid return labels at a reduced rate) save sales but complicate the accounting of what was sold and at what margin. How to apply: create separate accounts for return shipping and for return reprocessing, post coupons as revenue reductions, and in your contribution-margin model add return shipping and reprocessing per order using your actual return rate.
conditions: Brands with meaningful return rates (apparel, footwear); statutory accounts; confirm with your accountant.

topics: chart of accounts and P&L structure
claim: Accounting software usually receives only Shopify net revenue; report gross-to-net (refunds, discounts, shipping collected) monthly, or a revenue change cannot be explained.
body: Shopify splits gross sales into discounts, returns and shipping charges to reach net sales, but that breakdown typically does not flow into Xero or QuickBooks, which record only net or cash. Looking only at net in the accounts, a move from $100k to $110k could be anything. The speaker's example: gross revenue was $120k both months, refunds fell from $20k to $10k, and that alone explained the rise; in another case the difference was a discount code that ran one month and not the next. Gross-to-net lines are direct profit levers: lower refunds, fewer discounts, and collecting a little more shipping at checkout, which he says most stores under-collect. How to apply: add a monthly gross-to-net bridge (gross sales, discounts, refunds and chargebacks, shipping collected, net) to the management P&L from Shopify reports, alongside the accounting P&L, and set targets for refund and discount rates. Related P&L hygiene from the same source: interest on inventory loans goes below EBITDA, not in operating expenses; percentages for every P&L line should be tracked month to month.
conditions: Shopify brands whose bookkeeping imports summarised payouts or net sales into Xero, QuickBooks or similar.
fails_when: Setups whose connector already imports gross sales, discounts and refunds as separate lines; very small stores where the monthly bridge adds little.
numbers: example: gross $120k both months; refunds $20k -> $10k explained net $100k -> $110k

topics: funding options and cost of capital
claim: Inventory-funded growth is capped by the cash conversion cycle: agency-led tripling ($2M to $7M) financed by inventory loans repeatedly drove net profit to near zero.
body: When each purchase order must be paid from the gross profit of the last one, growth compounds slowly: sell 10 units, earn $50, buy 11; earn $55, buy 12. A 90-day lead time with full payment up front adds stockouts, because the next order cannot be placed until the last stock sells. The speaker has seen roughly five seven-figure brands whose agency scaled ad spend from about $20,000 to $200,000 a month and revenue from $2 million to $7 million a year while the founder quietly took millions in inventory financing; interest grew, marketing efficiency fell at higher spend, and net profit went to near zero, so founders who had been paid were no longer. His view: you cannot triple an inventory business in a year without large self-funding, outside capital or expensive debt, and growing slightly slower at better marketing efficiency with less interest often makes more money. Levers that relax the constraint: negotiate supplier terms (for example 20% deposit, balance on shipment, so a reorder can be placed after selling about two units), cut lead times (90 days to 30 with a different manufacturer), or use inventory financing knowingly, often with a personal guarantee. Put interest below EBITDA, not in operating expenses, so profit reads cleanly for buyers.
conditions: Inventory-holding DTC brands growing fast with paid media, especially sub-$10M revenue and dependent on lenders.
fails_when: Pre-order, print-on-demand or dropship models with little inventory float; brands with cheap equity capital; high-margin products whose gross profit funds reorders quickly.
numbers: ad spend $20k -> $200k/month; revenue $2M -> $7M/year; net profit -> near zero (about 5 cases seen)

topics: chart of accounts and P&L structure
claim: Price new products bottom-up: profit target plus opex sets a contribution target; add expected CAC, allowances, shipping and COGS; drop products the market will not pay for.
body: Keystone pricing (double the unit cost) and fixed markups (3x to 5x) ignore every variable cost of ecommerce and the market's price expectations; the speaker estimates about 40% of new brands use keystone and end up too thin to scale. Waterfall pricing works up from the profit you need. Example: a 10% net profit target plus 10% operating expenses means a 20% contribution margin target per order. Add expected CAC (say $30, from current account data), allowances for returns and discounts (say 3% each), shipping and fulfilment quoted by your carrier (say $11), and landed COGS (say $6), then solve for the price at which contribution is 20%; in his example about $70, not the $12 keystone would suggest. Then check competitors: if similar products sell at $30 to $40, either position this one as clearly premium in an uncontested space or do not launch it. Use the same P&L logic for diagnosis: set percentage targets for gross margin, MER, contribution and EBITDA, and when a line misses, look only at the lines above it for the cause.
conditions: DTC brands launching or repricing products sold mainly through paid acquisition.
fails_when: Marketplaces or retail-led brands with low CAC; loss-leader products deliberately priced to acquire customers for a high-LTV range; categories with strict price anchors where any premium fails.
numbers: keystone = 2x unit cost; about 40% of new brands price this way (estimate)
example: 10% net + 10% opex -> 20% contribution target; CAC $30, allowances 3% + 3%, shipping $11, COGS $6 -> about $70 price

claim: Push slow grade C/D inventory through paid media at break-even or a small loss, in isolated funnels or a new market, rather than cutting ad spend when cash is tight.
body: Profit is not cash: a brand reporting $2 million profit that bought $3 million of inventory that did not sell is $1 million cash negative. Inventory is graded A (fast), B (medium), C (slow) and D (not moving); Shopify can rank it. New product launches often sell 30 to 40% to the existing list, then stall, leaving cash trapped (one example had 400 days of stock on hand). Paid media teams KPI'd only on profit will never spend behind C and D stock because its ROAS is poor, so the stock sits. The speaker's alternative: deliberately fund C and D sell-through at break-even or a slight loss, in an isolated ad funnel, via whitelisted creator pages, or in a new country where heavy discounting will not erode brand equity in the main market. He also warns against the reflex CFO response in a slow month: when February revenue drops and MER rises from 25% to 30%, cutting media 40% can shrink revenue further; it may be right to raise MER temporarily (say from 30% to 35%) with the extra 5% dedicated to clearing C and D stock back into cash. Reduce SKU count as new products are added. Share the inventory position with the paid media team every month.
conditions: Inventory-holding DTC brands, especially fashion and multi-SKU catalogues, with stock aged beyond normal sell-through.
fails_when: Perishable or low-value stock where liquidation or bundling is cheaper than paid media; when marketing is not actually driving revenue, raising spend just deepens the loss; heavy discounting in the main market can train customers to wait.

MER 25% -> 30% in a slow month; temporary raise to 35% to clear C/D stock

claim: Calculate subscription CAC payback by cohort, not one customer: a 3.2-month naive payback became about 8 months once 25% churn by order two was included.
body: The common shortcut divides CAC by monthly gross profit per customer: $90 CAC over $28 monthly gross profit ($50 revenue minus $22 COGS) suggests payback in 3.2 months. It assumes nobody cancels. The correct method follows one monthly cohort: total CAC spent on everyone in the cohort goes out up front, and gross profit comes back only from those still active each month. In the worked example a July cohort of 3,500 customers cost $315,000 to acquire; retention was 100% at order one, 75% at order two and 50% at order three, falling to almost nothing by order 18. Cumulative gross profit only passed $315,000 in month 8, roughly two and a half times the naive figure, and the cohort barely made a profit after that. The same maths for a low-churn software business with $199 CAC moved payback from 7.1 to about 9 months (27% longer). Andrews says the payback figures founders quote are typically 20 to 100%, sometimes 200%, shorter than reality. For physical subscriptions with skips or every-other-month deliveries, measure payback in orders rather than months. Rerun with different CACs: in the low-churn case, $125 CAC broke even around month 5 and $225 around month 11.
conditions: Subscription or repeat-purchase businesses deciding how much to spend on acquisition; especially high-churn physical product subscriptions.

retention 75% at order 2, 50% at order 3 (high-churn example)
low-churn example 7.1 vs about 9 months (27% longer)

claim: Treat discounts and ad spend as one acquisition pool: a $60 discount that lifts conversion from 1.5% to 3.8% leaves profit per customer unchanged but can raise total profit 2.5x.
body: Eric Andrews' model: profit per first-time customer equals net order value minus COGS minus CAC, and the discount is just another acquisition cost, so add discount and CAC together. Worked example with identical inputs: $100,000 ad spend at $1.50 a click gives about 66,700 sessions; list price $200; COGS $75 ($50 product to warehouse, $25 fulfilment). No discount: 1.5% conversion, 1,000 buyers, CAC $100, $25 profit per customer after marketing. $30 off: assumed 2.2% conversion, 1,433 buyers, CAC $70, still $25 each. $60 off: assumed 3.8% conversion, 2,500 buyers, CAC $40, still $25 each, because discount plus CAC is $100 in every case. Total post-marketing contribution was $25,000, $36,000 and $63,000, so the deepest discount won in this scenario only because volume rose. The conversion lifts are assumptions; measure your own before copying. His rules: budget discounts and media from one annual pool and test the split; give the deepest discounts as the entry to a subscription or loyalty programme rather than a flash sale, since flash-sale buyers often never pay full price; and accept that sometimes fewer customers at better margins makes more money.
conditions: First-order economics for DTC brands with paid acquisition; requires measured conversion lift per discount level.
fails_when: The discount does not raise conversion enough to cut CAC by the same amount, or repeated deep discounts train customers to wait for sales and erode brand pricing.

$200 price, $75 COGS

post-marketing contribution $25,000 / $36,000 / $63,000

topics: chart of accounts and P&L structure
claim: Read the P&L in four buckets: cost of delivery 30-40% of revenue, variable media 40-50% for low-LTV goods, opex 10-12% for a strong brand, leaving 15-20% profit.
body: Holiday's 'four-quarter accounting' asks the accountant for one monthly view with four lines: cost of delivery (product cost plus variable costs per order such as pick and pack, shipping and payment fees), CAC (pure variable media spend; agency retainers and fixed creative staff go in opex, but creative bought per asset counts as variable), opex (rent, salaries, software and other fixed costs) and profit. His benchmarks: cost of delivery at 30 to 40% is rarely the main problem. Marketing as a share of revenue depends on LTV: a hard good with little repeat buying must buy most revenue new every month and runs 40 to 50% (Ridge runs about 50%); his portfolio's median first-purchase return on Meta for new customers is about 1.7, which implies acquisition cost of 55 to 60% of first-order revenue. High-LTV brands see this fall over time as returning customers fill revenue, and can afford more opex for service and retention. Opex for a great ecommerce brand has fallen from about 25% to 10 to 12%; above 20% he doubts a brand can compete. A 15 to 20% profit business is doing very well. Use the four lines to see which bucket is eating profit versus peers.
conditions: DTC ecommerce brands, roughly seven and eight figures; percentages are of net revenue; benchmarks from Common Thread Collective's client portfolio.

topics: chart of accounts and P&L structure
claim: Put inbound freight, duties and packaging in COGS; the source books outbound shipping to customers as a selling expense, so state which choice your P&L uses.
body: For a physical product business the source defines COGS as raw materials, direct labour, factory overhead (rent, depreciation, utilities, maintenance), inbound freight to bring materials or finished goods in, and the product's packaging. These costs sit on the balance sheet as inventory and move to the P&L as COGS only when the unit is sold. The misclassification the source sees most often is shipping: freight-in belongs in COGS, while freight-out (shipping orders to customers) is a selling cost and should sit in operating expenses. Other COGS distortions: expired or obsolete stock (sell nearest-expiry first, and clear stock at a markdown before it expires) and theft, which needs logged inventory in and out plus periodic counts. Why it matters for an ecommerce brand: gross margin feeds valuation and every unit-economics decision, and moving outbound shipping between COGS and operating expenses changes the gross margin percentage without changing profit. Whatever your accountant chooses, write the definition down, apply it every month, and when you calculate contribution margin per order still subtract outbound shipping, pick and pack and payment fees, wherever they sit on the P&L. Confirm the treatment with your accountant.
conditions: Physical product brands preparing a P&L, investor reporting or a gross margin benchmark comparison.
fails_when: Brands whose accountant includes outbound shipping and fulfilment in cost of sales, a disclosed policy choice many retailers make; comparisons across brands then need the same definition.

claim: Founders wanting a full exit should stay out of buyer meetings: if buyers see the founder as the brand's magic, they will insist the founder keeps a large stake.
body: The Salt & Stone founder's advice from two private equity processes. If you want to stay involved, attend the meetings and talk about your passion, because buyers want that energy. If you want to sell most or all of your equity, do the opposite: let the management team present. The moment a buyer concludes that the business depends on the founder, it will structure the deal so you retain a large share and stay on, which limits how much you can sell. The practical implication is to build a team that can run the business visibly before a sale: a CFO or president who has been through an acquisition, and leaders who own product, marketing and operations. In his own case he chose to stay and keep a large stake. This is a single founder's observation, not a rule about deal terms, and buyers will still do diligence on founder dependence through interviews and data.
conditions: Founder-led brands preparing for a majority sale to private equity or a strategic buyer.
fails_when: Brands where the founder genuinely is the product (founder-face brands), where hiding them is not credible; buyers who require founder rollover regardless.

topics: funding options and cost of capital
claim: Salt & Stone's sole owner took tens of millions off the table through a secondary PE sale while keeping control, choosing a firm that was not the top bidder.
body: Salt & Stone was profitable from launch (wholesale orders paid on shipment) and the founder owned 100%. His first liquidity event was a secondary transaction with a private equity firm: shares sold for cash to him personally, none to the company balance sheet, while he kept control. A second transaction with a larger firm followed within about 18 to 24 months. Selection criteria he used: a firm started by former founders (Humble Growth, led by Orgain's founder) who would let him keep running the brand; integrity and a shared long-term vision; spending personal time with the partners (dinners, a game, meeting his family). About 15 firms bid and he picked one that was not the highest offer, because some bidders seemed likely to push discounting or overrule brand decisions. Process notes: a good investment bank (Raymond James ran both deals); hire a CFO or president who has been through an acquisition, to prepare what a buyer will ask for; expect closing to stretch, his took the full 45-day window after being told two weeks. Revenue grew from about $16M to $29M to a $96-100M run rate under the first partner.
conditions: Profitable, founder-controlled brands with strong growth that want personal liquidity without selling control; US private equity market.
fails_when: Unprofitable or slow-growing brands that will not attract minority secondary interest; founders who need primary capital for the business rather than personal liquidity.

topics: funding options and cost of capital
claim: Keep a revolving credit line open for PO timing, use PO factoring for big retail orders (cheapest with blue-chip retailers like Costco or Walmart), and consider a debt recap.
body: Ridge never sold equity (it started on about $200,000 of Kickstarter pre-orders), but Frank says every business should have a debt revolver open. Uses: when a large purchase order drains cash, draw on the revolver to keep operations running, then repay when cash returns, and park excess cash in treasuries at other times. Factoring: when a retailer such as Target places a big PO with 90 to 120-day payment terms and you lack cash to produce it, a factoring lender advances money against that PO and is repaid when the retailer pays. Interest depends on the retailer's credit: a Costco or Walmart PO costs almost nothing, while a weak retailer's PO may not be financeable at all. A debt recapitalisation lets a profitable owner who has reinvested everything take money off the table, secured on the business rather than personally. How to apply: open the revolver while profitable (before you need it), map cash needs around each PO, and price factoring per retailer.
conditions: Profitable brands with inventory cycles and wholesale or retail customers; US lending market.
fails_when: Unprofitable or early brands that cannot secure a revolver; DTC-only brands with no POs to factor; debt recap that leaves the business over-levered for a downturn.

topics: funding options and cost of capital
claim: PE buyers want about 20% EBITDA growing about 20% a year plus a moat; conservative buyout debt is 2 to 3x EBITDA, and missing staff gets deducted from EBITDA.
body: Frank explains how most brand exits work: privately held brands usually sell to private equity first, and only later to a strategic acquirer (Dr. Squatch went through a PE owner before Unilever). PE wants a sustainable business matching its playbook: around 20% EBITDA margin growing about 20% a year for years, a moat (IP, retail relationships), strong cash flow, and visible upside ('meat on the bone') such as untapped retail, Amazon or a new customer segment, which the seller should point out. PE often finances deals as leveraged buyouts: in his example, a $100M purchase of a business with $20M EBITDA (5x) funded half by the fund and half by bank debt secured on the company. Two to three turns of EBITDA in debt is conservative; ZIRP-era deals used six or seven, which is how brands blow up after a sale. Buyers adjust EBITDA: a brand claiming 40% EBITDA with no team will be re-cut to something like 30% because the buyer must hire. Also understand deal terms such as participation and the 'second bite', which he says rarely pays off.
conditions: Profitable DTC brands considering a sale; US PE market; figures are one founder's rules of thumb.
fails_when: Strategic acquirers paying for a specific asset; venture-backed high-growth brands valued on revenue; very hot or very cold M&A markets.

topics: funding options and cost of capital
claim: IM8's $1B non-dilutive facility funds 70% of each month's marketing per cohort across 43 markets, repaid from that cohort's income, letting it tolerate 6-8 month CAC paybacks.
body: In July 2026 IM8 announced a $1 billion facility from the same lender model Lemonade (an insurer) used. Mechanics described by the speaker: each month IM8 can draw 70% of that month's marketing spend for the new cohort, across any channel in 43 markets; the loan is repaid from that cohort's subsequent income, paying less if the cohort pays back quickly and more if slowly. It is non-dilutive (no shares, warrants or convertibles), but the risk is not ring-fenced: if a cohort underperforms, IM8 still owes the money. Effect: cash needed to acquire a cohort falls by about 70% up front, which let IM8 report free cash flow positive and run first-order GP:CAC near 0.5 with 6 to 8 month payback, while unit profitability is unchanged. The speaker's caution: almost no brand can push payback to 6 to 8 months without such capital, and comparisons with Lemonade flatter IM8 because insurance retention over 2 to 4 years is far stickier than consumables. How to apply: if offered revenue-based or cohort-based marketing financing, model repayment under slower-than-expected cohort decay, confirm whether recourse extends beyond the cohort, and keep reporting profitability separately from cash.
conditions: Scaled DTC brands with proven, predictable cohort repeat curves considering cohort or revenue-based marketing finance.
fails_when: Brands with short histories or volatile retention, where cohort repayments can exceed cohort income; when repayment terms accelerate on underperformance; small brands for which such facilities are not available.

claim: True Classic financed growth with manufacturer net terms (up to net 90) and credit lines instead of equity; pitch suppliers your growth plan and honour the terms.
body: Bartlett says the first financing lever for a growing apparel brand is its production partner, where you have the most leverage. True Classic stayed bootstrapped by extending payment terms (net 30, then 60, then 90) and getting suppliers to extend credit, at one point betting on about $40M of inventory. The pitch to a supplier is concrete: 'we're doing $15M this year and will do $90M next year; do you want that business?' Suppliers can check the claim, since tools linked to Shopify and accounts show quickly whether the business is real. During a rough patch, moving to net 90 kept the company alive without another lever; one production partner later became an investor. His rules: you must be a credible storyteller, then actually deliver the revenue; if you run over agreed terms, compensate the supplier with interest or future volume. Bargaining power shifts once you are large: suppliers want you, rather than you chasing them. How to apply: model the cash conversion cycle, ask for longer terms in exchange for volume commitments, and keep supplier reporting honest.
conditions: Fast-growing, profitable or near-profitable brands with a concentrated supplier who benefits from their growth.
fails_when: New brands without a sales record; suppliers with tight cash themselves; missing the growth plan leaves you with stock and debt; terms extended without paying on time destroy the relationship.

claim: True Classic found standalone stores lost money; high-traffic mall stores cost $20,000 to $40,000 a month in rent and are judged on near break-even plus online halo.
body: Bartlett's retail lessons from nine owned stores plus a Target rollout: standalone locations chosen for customer density rather than foot traffic lost a lot of money; malls with heavy foot traffic work, but leases there can run $20,000, $30,000 or even $40,000 a month. A store's own profit and loss may not look good, so his target is to get each store's four-wall result close to break even and count the visibility it creates (people walking past signs, touching the product) as upper-funnel advertising, which should show up in post-purchase surveys. Some stores were profitable straight away, especially where they already had many online customers (Florida, which also predicted strong Target results). He started with a partner that stands up stores and staff for brands (Leap), which he suggests for testing one or two stores, and notes that one successful store gives you a case study to take to wholesale buyers. Plan: test, get near break-even, then scale to 50 to 100 stores over two years.
conditions: Established DTC brands with dense regional online customer bases considering physical retail; US malls.
fails_when: Brands without online density data; standalone locations; brands unable to fund losses during ramp-up.

claim: PE buyers underwrite IRR (often about 2x in roughly 2 years), strategic buyers underwrite earnings-per-share growth and synergy; model the business from each buyer's view.
body: Rahal, who sold RXBAR to Kellogg, describes the two buyer types differently. A private equity buyer paying, say, $300 million is focused on internal rate of return and will want at least about a 2x return within around two years, so it underwrites how many stores, how much revenue and what margin it can reach in that window; leveraged buyouts add debt to that maths. A strategic buyer such as a large food company thinks longer term and is judged by earnings per share, so it values synergies: putting your product into its distribution, international reach and topline growth that lifts EPS. His advice is to put yourself in each buyer's shoes and build the case they need to underwrite, rather than inflating projections ('don't perfume the pig'), because diligence uncovers everything. In the RXBAR process the team invited all interested strategics to the office and was fully transparent, which he credits with building trust. Investment bankers run the process; management sells the company. For an ecommerce brand planning an exit, keep clean financials and per-channel unit economics that let a buyer see both the near-term return and the synergy story.
conditions: Consumer brands with meaningful revenue considering a sale or recapitalisation; US M&A context.
fails_when: Small brands below the size PE or strategics buy, where exits are to individuals or aggregators with different maths; the 2x in 2 years figure is an illustration, not a market standard.

claim: Push slow grade C and D stock through its own paid funnel at break-even or a small loss to turn it into cash, rather than letting profit-ranked campaigns starve it.
body: Blue Sense Digital grades stock A (fast-moving), B (medium), C (slow) and D (not moving); Shopify can rank this for you. Product launches are a key growth lever but many fail, leaving stock that sold its first 30 to 40% through existing customers and then stalled. Example: a launch did $100,000 in sales against $1M of stock at sell value, leaving about 400 days of inventory on hand. A business can be profitable on paper and still lose cash: $2M profit with $3M of unsold inventory is $1M down in cash. Because agencies are judged on ROAS or profit, paid media never prioritises B to D stock, since it scores poorly. Their fix: put that stock into its own funnel and campaigns (in Meta, a separate funnel or whitelisted page; in Google, a dedicated campaign so a consolidated PMax does not give it zero spend) and run it at break-even or a slight loss. Once they moved a client's D stock into a new country where heavy discounting would not harm the main market's brand. Tell the media team the inventory position each month.
conditions: Brands carrying slow stock after launches or seasons; cash is the constraint rather than profit; media team able to run separate funnels.
fails_when: Stock is genuinely unsellable at any price (liquidate or write off instead); discounting in the main market would damage brand pricing; the brand is profit-constrained with ample cash.

claim: When unsold stock squeezes cash, cutting media often deepens the drop; temporarily raising marketing to revenue (example 30% to 35%) to clear C and D stock can restore cash.
body: Blue Sense Digital's CFO-versus-CMO example: in February, November stock is still unsold and cash is tight. The P&L shows cost of delivery about 30%, marketing about 25%, opex about 15% and profit about 30%. Revenue drops, marketing rises to about 30% of revenue, profit falls to about 25%, and the CFO cuts marketing by 40%. If marketing is what drives revenue, revenue then falls further, profit falls again, and the cycle repeats. Their counter-intuitive fix: lift marketing to about 35% of revenue for a short period, with the extra 5% aimed only at clearing grade C and D stock, accepting it is unprofitable, to convert stock back to cash and recover. They also see the reverse problem: about five times, a seven-figure brand's agency ramped spend from about $20,000 to $200,000 a month while the owner quietly took on millions in inventory financing, so interest costs ate the gains. The real limit was the cash conversion cycle (days inventory + days sales outstanding - days payables), not ad efficiency. Forecast new and returning revenue separately.
conditions: Brands where paid media drives most new revenue and cash is tied in inventory; seven to nine figure DTC; requires shared data between finance and marketing.
fails_when: Marketing is not actually driving revenue (cutting it would not reduce sales); no slow stock to clear; financing costs or covenants make any extra spend unaffordable.

claim: In a modelled ~$92k/month DTC brand, raising 30-day sell-through from 30% to 40% lifted cash from $50k to $70k with no change in net income.
body: The presenter models a bootstrapped DTC brand with about $92.5k monthly revenue, $30k monthly marketing, a $50k starting inventory and $50k cash. Even with positive net income the bank balance falls, because each month's inventory purchase leaves the account before the profit arrives; the cash conversion cycle, not profit, limits how fast the brand can grow. Three levers change cash without touching marketing. Sell-through: lifting 30-day sell-through from 30% to 40% (fewer slow SKUs, better purchasing) cuts reorders and moved ending cash from about $50k to $70k while net income stayed the same. Maintained markup: moving MMU from 4.0 to 4.5 through modest supplier negotiation and small price rises roughly doubled net income and cut inventory needed from about $55k to under $50k, moving cash to about $62k. Operating expenses: fixed costs flow one-for-one into net income, unlike variable marketing; cutting OpEx from $25k to $19k added about $6k a month. Applied together (OpEx $25k to $19k, MMU 4 to 4.5, sell-through 30% to 40%), monthly net income went from about $3.5k to $12.2k and cash from $50k to about $91k within the 60-day model. How to apply: model your own cash month by month and work two or three levers at once.
conditions: Inventory-holding DTC brands, bootstrapped or cash-constrained, ordering stock monthly against sell-through.
fails_when: Made-to-order or dropship models with little inventory; brands with long supplier lead times or MOQs that prevent smaller reorders; price rises that cut conversion more than markup gains; model outputs taken as forecasts without your own numbers.

claim: Judge CAC, AOV or repeat-rate improvements on 60 to 180-day cash, not 30 days; modelled, lifting repeat-revenue share from 25% to 35% added about $10k monthly net income.
body: The model's second lesson is timing. Improvements to customer acquisition cost, AOV or repeat rate compound through the inventory and reinvestment cycle, so a 30-day view understates them; the presenter says the effect shows over 60, 90 and 180 days. In the same modelled brand (about $92.5k monthly revenue), raising AOV from $150 to $180 with the same customers acquired and no extra fixed cost lifted monthly net income from about $2.6k to $16.3k, because gross profit grew while marketing and OpEx stayed flat. Raising the share of revenue from returning customers from 25% to 35% (more retention email, a better post-purchase experience) took revenue from about $98k to $113k and gross profit from about $60k to $69k, adding roughly $10k of net income, about five times the prior net cash flow. The presenter's reasoning: repeat purchases carry almost no acquisition cost, so returning customers drive 80 to 90% of profit in brands like this. How to apply: build a monthly cash model with inventory purchases, rank the six levers by the cash change each produces over 60 to 180 days, and attack the largest bottleneck first, rather than defaulting to more ad spend.
conditions: Bootstrapped DTC brands with repeat-purchase products and monthly inventory buying; teams able to model cash monthly.
fails_when: One-time-purchase categories with little repeat; brands where retention requires paid staff or agencies whose cost offsets the gain; numbers taken from the presenter's model rather than your own cohorts.
